{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Prompts\handoff_shotgun.md","content":"# Handoff: la escopeta (Glyphbound), con el mismo proceso que el rifle

**Para:** un chat nuevo de Claude Code en `C:\GameJam` (máquina CENTRAL).
**De:** el chat que rehízo el rifle el 2026-11-12 (bloques 18 a 23 y 25 de `Devlog/days/2026-11-12.md`).
**Antes de nada:** lee `CLAUDE.md`, `Devlog/README.md` y esos bloques de la bitácora: son la historia completa de lo que aquí se resume.

## El encargo
El dueño quiere para la escopeta lo mismo que se hizo con el rifle: un arma 3D en primera persona que se vea sólida y limpia, completa y funcional (gatillo, recarga animada, barra de energía, holograma de munición, luz de punto débil, fogonazo y retroceso), al nivel de la pistola y del rifle, que ya aprobó.

## Qué hay hoy
- **Datos:** la escopeta existe en `Glyphbound/Content/Data/Weapons.json` (`"Id": "Shotgun"`): 8 perdigones de 10, un disparo cada 0,8 s, 6 cartuchos, 4 cargadores de reserva, recarga de 2 s. **No tiene `"ViewModel"`**, así que en el juego se ve con formas provisionales.
- **Arte:** no hay nada de la escopeta en `Glyphbound/SourceArt/Weapons/` ni en `/Game/Glyphbound/Weapons/`.
  - En `C:\Users\VNasher\Downloads` hay un zip de Tripo reciente sin identificar (`tripo_convert_8f45a6e1-....zip`, del 12 nov 22:01: un FBX de 0,7 MB y una sola textura). **No sé si es la escopeta.** Pregunta al dueño cuál es el archivo fuente antes de abrir nada.
- **Código:** las dos armas reales comparten un solo camino en `Glyphbound/Source/Glyphbound/Weapons/GBGun.cpp`, descrito por una tabla de arte por modelo (`FGBGunModelArt`, constantes `PistolArt` y `RifleArt`, y la lista de `FindModelArt`). Añadir un tercer modelo es una constante nueva más una entrada en esa lista, **si el arma encaja en el contrato de abajo**.

## Contrato que el código espera de un modelo
**Mallas en `/Game/Glyphbound/Weapons/<Arma>/`**, todas obligatorias salvo la barra: si falta una, el juego avisa y vuelve a las formas provisionales.
- `SM_<Arma>_Body`: todo lo que no se mueve.
- `SM_<Arma>_Trigger`: origen en su bisagra.
- `SM_<Arma>_Magazine`: origen en su posición de reposo.
- `SM_<Arma>_WeakPointLight`: lo que se enciende al acertar en punto débil.
- `SM_<Arma>_AmmoDisplay`: un panel 2:1 mirando al jugador; U hacia la derecha del jugador.
- `SM_<Arma>_EnergyBar`: solo si la barra es una malla aparte (pistola). En el rifle va dentro del material del cuerpo.

**Ejes y unidades:** cañón hacia +X, origen del cuerpo en el punto de la mano (arriba de la empuñadura), 1 unidad = 1 cm.

**Parámetros de material que pone el juego** en todas las piezas: `ElementColor`; además `ImbueRemaining` (barra de energía de 13 celdas, según el UV 1), `Flash` (luz de punto débil) y `DisplayTexture` (holograma).

**El holograma lo dibuja el juego** si el modelo pone `bDrawDisplayFrame` (rifle): líneas de marco, número y un punto por bala. Con 6 cartuchos saldrán 6 puntos.

## Dos decisiones de diseño que la escopeta obliga a tomar
Son del arquitecto, pero cambian cómo se ve el arma, así que cuéntaselas al dueño en una sola pregunta y sigue con un valor provisional mientras responde.
1. **Recarga.** El código actual es de cargador: saca uno, mete otro y las balas llegan al final (`FinishReload`). Una escopeta clásica se carga cartucho a cartucho por un tubo.
   - Lo que no cuesta código: una escopeta de cargador de caja, que reutiliza la animación de recarga tal cual.
   - Lo que sí cuesta: cartucho a cartucho. Cambia la lógica de munición (recarga parcial, interrumpible) y la animación.
2. **Corredera.** Con 0,8 s entre disparos, lo natural es una corredera que va y vuelve tras cada tiro. Es una pieza móvil nueva (`SM_<Arma>_Pump`) y un movimiento nuevo en `UpdateViewModel`; el contrato de hoy no la tiene.

Everything any agent or person does on the project must be recorded here. If it is not in the dev log, it did not happen as far as the judges are concerned.

**Language:** the Official Rules (7(i)) require every part of the submission in English, and that includes the published dev log. When a day entry quotes a prompt written in Spanish, include the original and an English translation.

{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Devlog\days\2026-11-12.md","content":"## Sixteenth block: the assault rifle, from one Tripo mesh to a complete weapon
Owner's note (translated): "This is the game's assault rifle. I think it's a single mesh, and all the work it needs is ahead of it; you will do it. Animations, the colour change, the ammo panel, everything as you already know: it has to end up as a complete and absolutely functional weapon, with everything a game of this kind needs. Modify it in Blender or Unreal as you like. For code tasks, don't use Muse Spark, use Sonnet."

**The source.** The owner's `carabina-roja.zip` held a Tripo GLB. It is one mesh of about 1,000 loose panels and 5,498 triangles, 1.0 m long. It came with a 4096 albedo and a `neon_mask` that marks where it glows.
- It had **no magazine** and no separate moving parts.
- The architect (Claude Opus 5.5) did the art headless in Blender 5.3.0, without asking. Scripts:
  - `Tools/Blender/rifle_import_glb.py`: GLB to `SourceArt/Weapons/Rifle/Rifle.blend`, the one source;
  - `rifle_export_fbx.py`;
  - `Tools/Jam/Import-Rifle.ps1` and `import_rifle.py`, with the same one-source rule as the pistol.

**The parts and how each was chosen.** The rifle has five meshes in `/Game/Glyphbound/Weapons/Rifle`.
- **Trigger:** the blade's panels, picked by their bounding box inside the guard. Its origin is at the hinge, so it rotates -8° like the pistol's.
- **Magazine:** new geometry modelled by script, because the model had none and a rifle needs one to reload.
  - A curved box under the stub in front of the trigger guard, with a base plate.
  - A glowing slit on each side, in the element colour.
  - On reload it slides out 17 cm, then back in.
- **Weak-point light:** the two oval lenses on the sides of the sight. They are off normally and flash on a head or weak-point hit, the pistol's rule.
- **Ammo display:** a 2:1 hologram pane just behind the sight's eyepiece, facing the player. It is the pistol's shared `M_GunHolo`, with its own text layout: no frame or dots to avoid, so the number is larger.
- **Energy bar:** no separate mesh. The body's second UV map carries the position along the side neon strip, and `M_RifleAtlas` cuts the strip into 13 cells with thin dark gaps.
  - They drain from the muzzle end with the enchant's time left: the same "+ half a cell" rule and the same code as the pistol.
  - The rest of the neon glows in the element colour all the time: idle mint (the model's own colour), or the enchant's element.
- **Problems found by the import checks:**
  - The FBX import flips V, so the "on the strip" flag in UV 1 came out inverted. The check that counts strip vertices caught it.
  - The magazine's three material slots collapsed into one. A new check now requires 3 slots.
  - Both were fixed in the export script before any code used them.
- **Textures:** the 4096 maps are capped at 2048 in Unreal.

**Code: Claude Sonnet 5.5 at High effort.** The owner set it as the implementer for this chat, so not Muse Spark. Brief: `Prompts/feedback12_rifle_viewmodel.md`.
- The pistol-only viewmodel code became one code path for both guns. A small art description per model (folder, parts, offsets, scale, idle glow, muzzle tip, display layout) is chosen by `ViewModel` in `Weapons.json`.
- New for both guns:
  - **Shot kick:** the viewmodel moves back and tips up, then eases back over 0.09 s. It is the look only; aim and camera are untouched.
  - **Muzzle flash:** a 0.05 s glowing star at the muzzle in the glow colour.

  - half bar 0.52;

{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Devlog\days\2026-11-12.md","content":"## Eighteenth block: the rifle's look rebuilt in Blender, and a new top rail
The owner cut the rifle chat ("the weapon looks disgusting", "it looks made of jelly") and opened a new one (Claude Fable 5.2) with a handoff, `Prompts/handoff_rifle_look.md`. They also sent `carabina-roja.zip` again (translated): "I leave you the original zip and not the malformed version."

**The zip is the same model.** The architect opened its `model.glb` and the old `Rifle.blend` side by side in headless Blender: same node, 7,192 vertices, 5,498 triangles, same two textures. So the source was never swapped; the softness comes from what the source is and from how it was processed.
- Rendered untouched in Cycles from a first-person angle (`media/2026-11-12/14h_rifle_rebuild_before.png`), the GLB already reads soft:
  - it is a low-poly export whose one albedo carries baked light, grey smears and blurred edges;
  - it has no roughness, metallic, normal or AO map;
  - Tripo's own normals shade the flat panels as if they were dented.
- The earlier fixes made it worse in one way: roughness and metallic were derived from the albedo's brightness, so every smear in the texture became a patch of a different material.
- Welding the vertices showed the mesh is not really "1,000 loose panels": merged at 0.01 mm it is 14 pieces with 132 open edges. It was only split along UV seams.

**What was rebuilt, on the same shape** (`Tools/Blender/rifle_build_blend.py`, GLB → `Rifle.blend`, about 3 minutes):
- **Geometry:** vertices welded, Tripo's normals dropped, hard edges above 30°, then face-area weighted normals, so large flat panels shade flat.
- **Albedo:** every panel gets one flat tone. The script rasterizes the 1,024 panels into the atlas, takes each panel's median brightness and snaps it to a palette of four: white polymer, light grey, mid grey, dark metal. The baked light and the smears are gone.
  - The small drawn details (holes, panel lines) are kept and re-cut with crisp edges: texels much darker than their panel's median.
  - On mid-grey panels only strong contrast counts as a detail; weaker marks there were bake smears.
- **ORM:** roughness and metallic by tone, and an ambient-occlusion pass baked in Cycles.
- **Normal map:** baked in Cycles with a Bevel node (0.9 mm rounded edges, so edges catch light) and the drawn details pressed in 0.5 mm.
- **Neon mask:** edges re-cut. Under the neon the albedo is now near black, not the model's red, so the element colour reads clean.

**The top rail** (owner, translated: "On top of the rifle there are reliefs of consecutive black lines. In one part that pattern breaks. Fix that too."). A top-down render and the panel bounds showed why: the GLB's 17 rail teeth are between 7 and 34 mm long, with gaps of no fixed size.
- The 566 faces of the old rail are deleted and a new rail is modelled by the script: the same section and length, 23 equal teeth of 10 mm with 6.4 mm gaps, real chamfers, and its own flat dark-metal material slot.
- Before and after: `media/2026-11-12/14l_rifle_rail_before.png`, `14m_rifle_rail_after.png`.
- The body went from 5,409 to 7,435 triangles.

**Export and import scripts.**
- `rifle_export_fbx.py` no longer rebuilds the body through bmesh, which is what dropped the normals the first time. It copies the mesh data of `Rifle.blend` and moves it. Tested: the five FBX files and four textures come out, and the bounds and part offsets are the same as before, so the numbers in `GBGun.cpp` stay.
- `import_rifle.py` now builds `M_RifleAtlas` from the four textures (normal map with the green channel flipped, part of the AO multiplied into the albedo) and adds `MI_Rifle_Rail`. **It has not been run yet.**
- `rifle_import_glb.py` is deleted: the build script replaces it.

## Twenty-sixth block: the shotgun's source arrives, and what it is
The rifle chat left a handoff for the shotgun, `Prompts/handoff_shotgun.md`, and the owner opened a new chat (Claude Fable 5.2) with it and a zip from Tripo, `tripo_convert_8f45a6e1-….zip`. The handoff's first rule: inspect the source before touching it.

**What the zip holds** (`Tools/Blender/shotgun_inspect.py`, headless Blender 5.3.0, read-only): one FBX and one texture.
- One mesh of 20,957 triangles in 58 loose pieces, 1.03 m long. That is almost four times the rifle's triangle count, so the silhouette is better than the rifle's was.
- Tripo exported it turned 11.3° about the vertical axis. The bounding box said "27 cm wide", which made no sense for a gun; the top view showed it lying diagonally. The scripts turn it back (the angle that makes it narrowest: 13 cm).
- **One 2048 JPG colour texture and nothing else**: no roughness, metallic, normal, AO or emissive map. The colour carries baked light and a frost-like painted wear. It is the same kind of source that made the rifle look "made of jelly", at half the rifle's texture size.
- 1,391 open edges: some show as black gaps on the stock from the player's side.
- What it shows: a science-fiction shotgun with a barrel over a tube, a ribbed forend, a glowing blue cell in front of the receiver, a screen on each side, exposed wires and a circuit board, a holographic sight with a rear window, a trigger, a thumbhole stock and cyan glow strips.

**Rendered untouched from the player's camera first** (`Tools/Blender/shotgun_render_review.py`, adapted from the rifle's; Cycles). The first try put the eye where the rifle's script has it, and the thumbhole stock, which rises 15 cm above the grip, filled the frame. The eye went up over the stock's comb.
- `media/2026-11-12/17a_shotgun_source_first_person.png`: the shape reads well; the sight's rear window faces the player.
- `17b_shotgun_source_close.png`, `17d_shotgun_source_screen.png`: up close the texture is blurred, the screens' glyphs are smudges and the parts nearest the camera are the softest.
- `17c_shotgun_source_left.png`: the whole gun from the left.

**Told to the owner at once**, as the handoff asks: a re-export from Tripo with PBR maps and a 4K texture would be cheaper than rebuilding the look from one 2K colour JPG. No credits are spent without the owner's say.

**How the model maps onto what the game needs** (architect's provisional choices, put to the owner in one question):
- **Reload:** the glowing blue cell is the magazine. It slides out, a fresh one goes in. This reuses the reload animation and the ammunition code as they are. Shell-by-shell loading would change the ammunition logic and is not planned unless the owner asks for it.
- **Pump:** the ribbed forend slides back and forward after each shot. It is a new moving part and a small new motion in the gun code; with 0.8 s between shots there is time for it, and it is what makes a shotgun read as one.
- **Ammo display:** a hologram in the sight's rear window, which already faces the player. The side screens are seen almost edge-on from the first-person camera.
- **Weak-point light**, **energy bar:** the sight's small indicator and the cyan strip on the handguard; to be confirmed on the mesh.

**Not imported into Unreal.** The source sits in `Glyphbound/SourceArt/Weapons/Shotgun/` (outside git, README tracked).
- **Implementer exception:** done by the architect directly, not Muse Spark: reading renders and deciding on them.

## Design decisions

{"file_path":"C:\GameJam\Tools\Blender\shotgun_pieces.py","content":"# Lists the shotgun's loose pieces in the straightened frame (muzzle -Y, up +Z, gun centred on X = 0, metres) and
# renders chosen groups highlighted in red on a grey gun, to find the moving parts (trigger, cell, forend, sight).
# Piece numbers are stable: pieces are sorted by vertex count, then by their lowest vertex index.
# Usage: blender -b --factory-startup --python shotgun_pieces.py -- <model.fbx> <out_dir> ["3,4;7;12,13" groups]
import bpy, bmesh, sys, os, math, glob
import numpy as np
from mathutils import Vector

argv = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--") + 1:]
fbx, out_dir = argv[0], argv[1]
groups = [[int(i) for i in g.split(",")] for g in argv[2].split(";")] if len(argv) > 2 and argv[2] else []
os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
bpy.ops.wm.read_factory_settings(use_empty=True)
bpy.ops.import_scene.fbx(filepath=fbx)
ob = [o for o in bpy.data.objects if o.type == "MESH"][0]
bpy.context.view_layer.objects.active = ob
ob.select_set(True)
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(location=True, rotation=True, scale=True)
me = ob.data
xy = np.array([v.co[:2] for v in me.vertices])
width, yaw = min((np.ptp(xy[:, 0] * math.cos(a) - xy[:, 1] * math.sin(a)), a) for a in np.radians(np.arange(-25, 25, 0.05)))
ob.rotation_euler.z = yaw
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(rotation=True)
xs = [v.co.x for v in me.vertices]
ob.location.x = -(min(xs) + max(xs)) / 2
bpy.ops.object.transform_apply(location=True)
print("STRAIGHTEN yaw_deg", round(math.degrees(yaw), 2), "width", round(float(width), 4))

bm = bmesh.new()
bm.from_mesh(me)
bm.verts.index_update()
seen, pieces = set(), []
for v in bm.verts:
    if v.index in seen:
        continue
    stack, vs = [v], []
    seen.add(v.index)
    while stack:
        a = stack.pop()
        vs.append(a)
        for e in a.link_edges:
            b = e.other_vert(a)
            if b.index not in seen:
                seen.add(b.index)
                stack.append(b)
    pieces.append(vs)
pieces.sort(key=lambda vs: (-len(vs), min(v.index for v in vs)))
piece_of_face = {}

questions.question: La escopeta de Tripo trae una sola textura de color JPG de 2048, sin rugosidad, metálico ni normales, y de cerca se ve borrosa (igual que el rifle al principio). ¿Puedes reexportarla de Tripo con texturas PBR en 4K (mejor en GLB)?

options.label: La reexporto (Recommended)
options.description: Me pasas el nuevo zip y trabajo sobre él. Es lo que mejor queda y lo que menos horas cuesta. Si Tripo pide créditos para la textura HD, eso lo decides tú.

options.label: Sigue con esta
options.description: Reconstruyo el aspecto por script en Blender como con el rifle: soldar, normales, tonos limpios, oclusión y relieve horneados. Varias horas y varias rondas de renders, y el detalle fino seguirá limitado por el JPG de 2048.

questions.question: ¿Cómo se recarga la escopeta? El modelo tiene una célula azul brillante delante del gatillo y no tiene cargador de caja.

options.label: Célula de energía (Recommended)
options.description: La célula azul sale, entra una nueva y llegan los 6 cartuchos al final. Reutiliza la animación y el código de recarga de la pistola y el rifle tal cual.

options.label: Cartucho a cartucho
options.description: Recarga clásica de escopeta: uno a uno, parcial e interrumpible al disparar. Cambia la lógica de munición y necesita una animación nueva; cuesta bastante más.

questions.question: ¿La escopeta lleva corredera que va y vuelve tras cada disparo (hay 0,8 s entre tiros)?

options.label: Sí, con corredera (Recommended)
options.description: El guardamanos estriado de abajo se desliza y vuelve tras cada tiro, y el arma acompaña con un gesto. Es una pieza móvil nueva y un movimiento nuevo en el código (pequeño). Es lo que hace que se lea como escopeta.

options.label: No, solo retroceso
options.description: Dispara como la pistola y el rifle: retroceso y fogonazo, sin pieza nueva. Sin coste de código.

El GLB nuevo es la misma escopeta con la textura de color al doble de resolución, pero **sigue sin mapas PBR**, y los cables son la parte más floja de la textura. No he reconstruido ni importado nada todavía.

## La textura
- **Qué cambió:** el color pasa de un JPG de 2048 a uno de 4096 (31 téxeles por cm sobre el arma). La malla es idéntica: 20.957 triángulos, mismos UV y el mismo giro de 11,3° con que la exporta Tripo.
- **Qué falta:** el material solo trae color. No hay rugosidad, metálico, normales, oclusión ni emisivo, así que todo se comporta como plástico mate y las tiras y pantallas cian están pintadas, no brillan.
- **Qué lleva pintado dentro:** luz y sombras, un desgaste tipo escarcha en los bordes y parches rectangulares de tono distinto donde se juntan dos proyecciones.
- **Malla:** hay 1.392 bordes abiertos; uno se ve como un hueco negro en el lomo de la culata, del lado del jugador.

## Los cables
- **Son geometría real**, no pintura: tres mazos (izquierda del cajón, y uno a cada lado del guardamanos) más un lazo corto junto a la pantalla. Suman unos 7.000 triángulos, un tercio del arma.
- **Forma:** cada mazo son varios hilos fundidos entre sí, de unos 3 mm, con sección de 4 a 6 lados, quebrados, aplastados como cintas en algunos tramos y atravesándose.
- **Color:** ningún hilo tiene color propio. Son del gris azulado del cuerpo, con cobre-naranja en solo el 3 % al 7 % de sus téxeles, a parches a lo largo de cada hilo.
- **Mancha en el cuerpo:** el cuerpo que queda detrás lleva impresa la mancha naranja y la sombra pintada de los cables (se ve en el render sin luz del mazo delantero).
- **Desde tu cámara** el mazo del cajón queda a la vista, en el costado izquierdo y cerca del ojo, así que importa.

## Lo que haría con los cables
1. Separarlos del cuerpo con su propio material.
2. Dar un color limpio a cada hilo: goma negra, rojo oscuro, cobre y azul, que son los que la textura insinúa.
3. Redondearlos con sombreado suave y un nivel de subdivisión.
4. Acabado de goma, sin luz pintada.
5. Borrar su mancha del cuerpo y hornear una sombra de contacto real.

El resto del aspecto lo derivo por script como en el rifle (rugosidad y metálico por zonas, normales y oclusión horneadas, máscara de brillo sacada del cian). Si tu modelo en Tripo tiene la opción PBR activada al texturizar, esa exportación me ahorraría parte; si no la tiene, exportar de nuevo no la añade.

## Tus decisiones, ya en el GDD (v0.33)
- **Recarga cartucho a cartucho:** la reserva se cuenta en cartuchos (24), cada uno tarda 0,33 s (la recarga completa sigue en 2 s), y disparar la interrumpe. Los números son provisionales.
- **Corredera:** el guardamanos estriado se mueve tras cada tiro, solo como efecto visual. En el modelo tiene la célula azul justo detrás, así que el recorrido lo decido al cortar la pieza.

La copia FBX anterior la borré del proyecto (queda `model.glb` como única fuente); tus dos archivos en Descargas siguen intactos. El código de la recarga y la corredera aún no está empezado.

# Measures the shotgun where parts have to be modelled on it, by casting rays at the built Shotgun.blend (frame:
# muzzle -Y, up +Z, X = 0 on the centre line, metres; printed in millimetres):
#   top      the height of the top surface along the gun (receiver block, stock comb), on three lines
#   bottom   the height of the underside between the cell and the trigger guard (the loading port's place)
#   forend   cross-sections of the lower front (how far out the left side is at each height, and the underside)
#   sight    the depth of the sight's rear, seen from behind (its window and its lower panel)
# Usage: blender -b --factory-startup --python shotgun_measure.py -- <Shotgun.blend>
import bpy, sys
from mathutils import Vector
from mathutils.bvhtree import BVHTree

argv = sys.argv[sys.argv.index("--") + 1:]

La escopeta está reconstruida y con sus piezas funcionales modeladas; te mandé dos tandas de renders (el aspecto, `17j`–`17n`, y las piezas, `17o`–`17u`). No está importada a Unreal: espero tu visto bueno.

## Qué cambió respecto a la fuente
- **Cables:** separados del cuerpo, cada pieza con un color limpio (negro, cobre, rojo oscuro, azul), redondeados y sin luz pintada. La mancha que dejaban en el cuerpo ya no está.
- **Cuerpo:** un único azul marino sacado del propio modelo, sin escarcha ni luz horneada, con aristas duras y relieve y oclusión horneados.
- **Carbono:** la trama original estaba demasiado borrosa para recortarla, así que la redibujé regular (rombos de 3 mm) sobre los mismos paneles.
- **Brillo:** las tiras, los glifos de las pantallas y la célula emiten de verdad. La célula es ahora un cilindro modelado con tres anillos, porque la original era irregular.
- **Otro tono:** la mira en metal más oscuro, el gatillo en acero y la cantonera en goma, para que no sea todo un mismo azul.

## Piezas funcionales
- **Holograma de munición:** en la ventana trasera de la mira, de cara a ti, con el número y un punto por cartucho.
- **Barra de energía:** 13 celdas sobre el bloque del cajón, justo detrás de la mira.
- **Luz de punto débil:** una lente bajo la ventana de la mira, apagada hasta que el juego la encienda.
- **Puerto de carga y cartucho:** una abertura enmarcada en la cara inferior, delante del guardamonte.
- **Corredera:** un manguito estriado alrededor del guardamanos, que retrocede 42 mm y vuelve.
- **Gatillo:** separado, con la bisagra arriba.

En total son 37.638 triángulos (la fuente tenía 20.957) en seis objetos.

## Límites que verás en los renders
- Los paneles de carbono tienen el contorno redondeado, no los trapecios nítidos del original.
- Los glifos de las pantallas laterales siguen siendo los signos inventados de Tripo, solo recortados.
- La placa de circuito quedó casi toda azul; solo conserva algo de verde.
- El hueco oscuro en el lomo de la culata es del propio modelo y sigue ahí.

## Qué falta
- Scripts de exportación e importación a Unreal (los del rifle sirven de plantilla).
- Código: recarga cartucho a cartucho y movimiento de la corredera. Como pediste para este frente, se lo encargo a Sonnet.
- Después: comprobación automática sin PIE, empaquetado, y que alguien lo juegue.

La fuente está en `Glyphbound/SourceArt/Weapons/Shotgun/` (`model.glb` y `Shotgun.blend`); el proceso completo, con las cinco ideas que fallaron antes de dar con esta, está en el bloque 29 de la bitácora.

Apliqué tus dos notas y después hice la revisión por zonas que pediste: capturé diez zonas del arma, encontré siete defectos y los corregí. Los siete renders de la serie `18a`–`18g` sustituyen a los cinco que te mandé antes de revisar; aquella entrega salió sin esa pasada y fue un error mío.

## Tus dos notas

- **Célula:** las medidas confirmaron lo que veías. Mi cilindro era más gordo que el hueco y atravesaba las piezas vecinas. Las dos paredes del hueco están inclinadas 14° y 20°, y un cilindro de tapas rectas las cortaba en diagonal. Además era un tubo liso sin nada que lo sujetara. Ahora es un cartucho asentado, con collares metálicos que entran en las dos paredes, vidrio más fino con brillo uniforme, dos abrazaderas, cuatro varillas, una montura bajo el cañón y dos apoyos. La célula original de Tripo la borré de la malla.
- **Panel lateral:** ya no es una pantalla. Es una placa con borde grabado, un tornillo en cada esquina, tres ranuras y un sello abstracto incrustado (un rombo con otro dentro y una barra a cada lado). El sello brilla con el color del encantamiento, como el resto del arma; si lo prefieres apagado, es un valor.

## Lo que encontré y cambié en mi revisión

1. **Paneles de carbono:** tenían contorno irregular, "mordiscos" azules dentro y retales sueltos en los tubos. Ahora son polígonos de bordes rectos, iguales a ambos lados.
2. **Tira de la culata:** su extremo delantero era una mancha rasgada, justo en tu vista. Quedó recortada a su ancho.
3. **Panel pequeño junto a los cables:** seguía con un signo de pantalla. Ahora es una plaquita con el mismo rombo.
4. **Dos bultos azul y negro** junto a ese panel: eran trozos cortos de cable. Ahora son negros y se leen como conectores.
5. **Placa de circuito:** era un borrón verde de baja resolución. La quité; esa zona queda en el azul del arma.
6. **Manchas fantasma** en el guardamanos y motas oscuras sueltas en la mira: eliminadas.
7. **Raya oscura rota** sobre el panel delantero de la culata: eliminada.

## Lo que sigue imperfecto

- El panel trasero de la culata conserva un mordisco azul junto a la cantonera, y su contorno tiene bastantes esquinas.
- Los trozos cortos de cable siguen siendo bultos, solo que negros.
- Algunas puntas de cable en la ranura del guardamanos terminan en el aire.

You implement one part of **Glyphbound**, a first-person RPG shooter for the Epic AI MegaJam 2026, in **Unreal Engine 5.9.0**, C++. The architect (another agent) wrote the public headers; you write the implementation. Several implementers work **at the same time** on different folders, so the rules about file ownership matter.

## Read before writing
1. `C:\GameJam\Design\ARCHITECTURE.md` (the whole file, it is short).

3. In `C:\GameJam\Glyphbound\Source\Glyphbound\`: `Core/GBTypes.h`, `Core/GBStatNames.h`, `Core/GBPlaceholder.h`, `Data/GBDataTypes.h`, `Data/GBDataSubsystem.h`, `Stats/GBStatsComponent.h`, `Stats/GBAttributeComponent.h`, `Combat/GBCombatLibrary.h`, plus every header your task names. The header comments are the specification: implement what they say.

## File ownership
- You own ONLY the files listed in your task. Create the `.cpp` for each header you own, and new files inside your folders if you need them.
- **Never edit a file you do not own.** If you need something from another module that its header does not offer, code against what exists, and write the request in your final report.
- In headers you own you MAY add includes, private/protected members, helper methods and extra public methods. You MUST NOT remove, rename or change the signature of anything already public there: other implementers are calling it right now.
- Do not edit `Glyphbound.Build.cs`, `.uproject`, or `Config/`. Module dependencies available: Core, CoreUObject, Engine, InputCore, EnhancedInput, Json, JsonUtilities, AIModule, NavigationSystem, Slate, SlateCore, UMG. If you need another one, say so in your report.

## Hard rules
- **Do not build, do not run the Editor, do not run tests, do not commit, do not launch other agents.** The architect integrates and builds after everyone finishes. Write code that compiles: check every engine API you are not sure about in the engine source at `C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.9\Engine\Source` (grep the header). UE 5.9 is newer than your training data; when in doubt, look.
- **No gameplay numbers in code.** Damage, costs, cooldowns, speeds, sizes, durations, timings and counts come from the JSON data through `UGBDataSubsystem` and `UGBStatsComponent` (stat names in `Core/GBStatNames.h`). If you need a number that has no stat yet, add a named constant `inline const FName` in a header YOU own (same style as `GBStatNames.h`), read it from the data with a sensible default, put its value in your JSON file, and list it in your report. Layout pixels and pure visual offsets may be code constants.
- Everything must work when a JSON entry is missing: use the default argument, log a warning with `UE_LOG(LogGB, Warning, ...)`, never crash, never divide by zero.
- No binary assets. 3D placeholders: `GBPlaceholder::SetupShape` (engine basic shapes). Pixel-art placeholders: `UGBPixelSpriteLibrary` (sprites described as text in `Sprites.json`). Art rule (GDD 3): medieval and magic things are pixel-art sprites; cyberpunk things are 3D.

- Do not keep pointers to definitions (`FGBSpellDefinition*`...) across frames; keep the id.
- A class member must never be named `Cast` (it hides the engine's `Cast<T>()`).
- All on-screen text in English. Comments in English, and only where they explain a decision or a non-obvious rule. ASCII only.
- Includes are relative to the module root: `#include "Stats/GBStatsComponent.h"`. Every `.cpp` includes its own header first. Every header with reflected types includes its `.generated.h` last.
- Keep it simple. This is a 4-day jam: clear, short code that works beats clever code. No speculative abstractions beyond what the headers define.

{"type":"text","file":{"filePath":"C:\GameJam\Design\ARCHITECTURE.md","content":"# Glyphbound: code architecture

> Written by the architect (Claude Code) on 2026-11-12. Source of truth for how the C++ is organized.
> Design lives in `Design/GDD.md`; this file says how the code implements it. Keep it short and current.

## Principles
1. **Data, not code.** Every gameplay number lives in `Glyphbound/Content/Data/*.json` and is read through `UGBDataSubsystem`. Code never hardcodes damage, costs, speeds, durations, sizes or timings. The JSON ships as loose files, so numbers can be tuned in a packaged build with a text editor (`gb.ReloadData` reloads while playing).
2. **One stat system.** A number is a *named stat*: base value from data, then modifiers. `UGBStatsComponent` evaluates `(Base + adds) * multipliers` (or an override). Skill-tree nodes, armor, status effects, air passives and the weapon enchant are all just groups of modifiers with a source name. Nothing else changes numbers.
3. **One damage path.** Everything that hurts goes through `UGBCombatLibrary::DealDamage(Target, FGBDamageInfo)`. Shields, resistances, teams, on-hit effects and kill credit hook in there once.
4. **Spells are data + a behavior.** A spell is a `FGBSpellDefinition` (params with `Base/Min/Max/ScaledBy`) plus the class of an `AGBSpellActor` behavior. The QTE result (power, reach) scales the params tagged for it. A new spell that fits an existing behavior is a JSON entry, no code.
5. **Shared pieces.** One projectile (`AGBProjectile`) for staff bolts, spell projectiles, enemy shots and grenades. One status-effect component for slows, burns, potions and buffs. One interact interface for portals, chests, pickups and the seal.
6. **Text in git.** No binary assets are required to run: input actions, the test arena, placeholder shapes and placeholder pixel sprites are all built in C++ from text. `Content/` is ignored by git except `Content/Data/`.
7. **No GAS.** Unreal's Gameplay Ability System was considered and rejected for the jam: it needs a lot of boilerplate and asset setup, and the game's needs (costs, cooldowns, timed effects, stat upgrades) are covered by principles 2-4 in a few hundred lines we fully control.
8. **PIE is human-only.** Agents build, run the pure-logic tests and package; a person plays.

<#
Smoke-Jam.ps1 - Runs the game by itself (console command "gb.Smoke": a scripted run of the main systems that
takes screenshots and quits) and reports what happened. It is NOT Play In Editor and nobody plays: it only
tells us whether the game starts, the systems run without crashing, and what the screen looks like.
A person still has to play the build.

Usage:
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/Smoke-Jam.ps1              # uncooked game with the Editor binaries (-game)
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/Smoke-Jam.ps1 -Packaged    # the packaged build in Glyphbound/Build/Windows
  powershell -File Tools/Jam/Smoke-Jam.ps1 -Only Entity -Offscreen   # only the Entity steps, no window
Output: the SMOKE lines, errors and warnings of our log category, and the list of screenshots.
Exit code: 0 = the script reached "SMOKE DONE" with no error lines and no crash.
#>
param(
    [switch]$Packaged,
    [string]$Only = '',      # filtered run: only the steps whose name starts with this (for example Entity), then quit
    [switch]$Offscreen,        # adds -RenderOffscreen: no window pops up
    [string]$Project = (Join-Path $PSScriptRoot '..\..\Glyphbound\Glyphbound.uproject'),
    [string]$EngineDir = 'C:\Program Files\Epic Games\UE_5.9',
    [int]$TimeoutSeconds = 180
)
$Project = (Resolve-Path $Project).Path
$projDir = Split-Path $Project -Parent
$stamp = [DateTime]::UtcNow.ToString('yyyyMMdd-HHmmss')
$smokeCmd = if ($Only) { "gb.Smoke $Only" } else { 'gb.Smoke' }
$common = @('-windowed', '-ResX=1280', '-ResY=720', '-unattended', '-nosplash', '-nosound', "-ExecCmds=`"$smokeCmd`"")
if ($Offscreen) { $common += '-RenderOffscreen' }
if ($Packaged) {
    $exe = Join-Path $projDir 'Build\Windows\Glyphbound.exe'
    if (-not (Test-Path $exe)) { Write-Host "No packaged build at $exe"; exit 2 }

## Tiempo de iteración (el tiempo premia en este proyecto)
- **Plugins:** el proyecto se crea con los plugins que ya trae el motor por defecto **desactivados si no se usan**, porque alargan el arranque y la compilación. Se dejan solo los que el juego o el flujo necesitan (el MCP, Enhanced Input, el de DLSS si se usa, Paper2D si se usa para sprites, etc.). Se mide el arranque del Editor antes y después.
- **Compilar poco:** cambios solo en `.cpp` con Live Coding; build completo solo cuando cambian cabeceras, `UPROPERTY`/`UFUNCTION` o módulos. Una compilación o corrida a la vez por máquina.
- **No correr la suite entera en cada cambio:** en cada cambio, solo el filtro anclado de lo que se tocó. La suite completa (por debajo de 30 s) una vez antes de empaquetar al final del día.
- **Arranque del Editor:** mapa inicial casi vacío, `bEnableUncontrolledChangelists=False` y, en corridas sin ventana, `-unattended -nopause -nosplash -NullRHI -nosound -nocrashreports` (detalles en `Devlog/PREJAM_PREP.md`, "Where the time really went").

All five review points are fixed. Editor build Succeeded, the five weapons tests pass (5 run, 0 failed), and the filtered smoke ends `Smoke: done=True crashed=False LogGB errors=0 timedOut=False wall=31 s` (31 steps).

Lock file: the rule arrived after my last build, test and smoke runs had finished. I never created `Saved\machine.lock`, never had to wait for it, and left nothing to delete. I did not touch the uproject or Plugins.

Changes (files: Weapons/GBGun.h, GBGun.cpp, Tests/GBWeaponsTests.cpp, Core/GBDevCommands.cpp):

1. A tap on an empty reload keeps its shot. `StopPrimary()` no longer clears `bFireWhenLoaded`. The pending shot is now cleared only on unequip, `SetAmmo`, `RefillAmmo`, a cancelled reload, and death (checked each tick in the per-round branch).

2. Pressing fire interrupts the reload at once. `StartPrimary()` is now a real override in GBGun.cpp.
   - If a per-round gun is reloading and has rounds in the gun, it calls `CancelReload()` immediately; the shot then follows through `PressTrigger` as soon as the fire rules allow.
   - If the gun is empty and reloading, it sets the pending shot.
   - Magazine guns still go straight to `PressTrigger()`, as before.

3. A pending shot loads exactly one shell.
   - `FGBPerRoundReload::Advance` has a new `MaxRounds` argument (default `MAX_int32`), and it keeps the leftover time when the cap stops it.
   - `Tick` passes 1 while a shot is pending. When that first shell lands it calls `CancelReload()` and queues the shot (`bAttackQueued`), so the reload stops even if the fire cooldown is still running.

4. The hands no longer jump on a cancel. `BeginReloadBlend()` now captures `ReloadBlendPoseAmount`, and the blend sets `CurrentPoseAmount = ReloadBlendPoseAmount * Left`.
   - Only per-round guns read that value (`GetReloadHandBeat` and `GetReloadPoseAmount`), so the pistol's and rifle's cancelled reloads use the same numbers as before.
   - I did not run a pistol or rifle smoke, so this is by code reading only.

5. The four tests are tightened.
   - `PerRoundFullReload`: steps to exactly `ReloadTime`, with 1 ms-before checks at the first cycle and at the end. Complete at 2.0 s, not complete 1 ms before.
   - `PerRoundShortReserve`: checks nothing moves 1 ms before `ReloadTime/MagazineSize`, then lands exactly at it.
   - `PerRoundLongFrame`: asserts the remainder and counts across three calls (0.4 kept, 0.4+0.5 gives 0.9 with no move, +0.2 gives one round with 0.1 left). It also covers the `MaxRounds=1` case: a 3.4-cycle step moves exactly one round and keeps 2.4 cycles.
   - `PerRoundStopPartWay`: checks the first shell's boundary (nothing 1 ms before one cycle, one round at it) before the part-way stop.
   - Test names are unchanged: Glyphbound.Weapons.PerRoundFullReload, PerRoundShortReserve, PerRoundLongFrame, PerRoundStopPartWay (plus the existing SnapshotSlots).
   - I did not run the old implementations against the new tests to confirm each wrong version now fails.

New smoke checks in the shotgun block:
- Tap on an empty gun during its reload: the first shell lands and the shot is fired (23 rounds in all, last shot 0.16 s ago). It errors if the shot is lost.
- Fire pressed inside the cooldown: shoot, start a reload, press fire. The press stops the reload at once (reloading 1 then 0, ammo 2/24). It errors if the reload keeps running.
- The cancel step now follows these two (it uses `SC = SP + 1.0f`).

Not verified:
- The HUD hand blend after a cancel, by eye.
- The full smoke, which I did not run.
- The empty-gun path with a very long frame in a live game (only unit-tested via `MaxRounds`).
- ShotgunArt framing is untouched.

- **Recarga:** entra un cartucho cada 0,33 s; la reserva se cuenta en cartuchos y el HUD muestra "x24 shells". Disparar corta la recarga en el momento. Con el arma vacía basta un toque: entra el primer cartucho, se corta la recarga y dispara.

- **Resto:** el holograma de la mira muestra el número y los seis puntos, la luz de punto débil se enciende en cabeza y la barra de energía sigue al encantamiento.

- **Prueba automática completa** (una sola vez, al final): 138 pasos, 0 errores, sin caídas. Las 38 líneas de la pistola y el rifle son idénticas a la corrida anterior.

- **Barra de energía:** en el cajón, como decidiste, se ve de canto y apenas se lee.
